Learning Objectives

After this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Turn real-world counts into probabilities using natural frequencies
  • Read and build lookup tables (Conditional Probability Tables) that capture how parent variables shape a child variable
  • Use Bayes’ rule to think backwards – “we see a bad outcome; what probably caused it?”
  • Explain why each node in a Bayesian network only depends on its direct parents and why that simplifies everything
  • Build and query a Bayesian network in R using bnlearn

Chapter Overview – From Arrows to Numbers

Where we are: In Chapters 2 and 3 we built qualitative causal models – diagrams with arrows and [+]/[-] signs. Those diagrams tell us what affects what and in which direction. But they cannot tell us by how much. This chapter adds numbers.

Think of it this way: a qualitative model is like a road map that shows which towns are connected. A quantitative model adds the distances between towns – now you can actually plan a trip.

Counting to Probability

Start with what you can count

Start with Counts

The most natural way to think about uncertainty is to count things.

Tanzania Health Facilities

Tanzania has roughly 8,000 health facilities across 26 regions. The country faces a workforce shortage estimated at about 55% (WHO/Lancet). So:

  • Out of 100 health facilities in rural Tanzania, about 55 have a severe workforce shortage.
  • The other 45 have staffing closer to what is needed.

That is a fact you can picture: line up 100 facilities, and more than half are short-staffed.

These counts – “55 out of 100” – are called natural frequencies. They are easier to reason with than abstract decimals, so we will use them as our starting point throughout this chapter.

From Counts to Probability

Probability is just a shorthand for natural frequencies.

Natural Frequency Probability
55 out of 100 facilities are short-staffed P(Staffing = Low) = 0.55
45 out of 100 facilities have adequate staffing P(Staffing = Adequate) = 0.45
20 out of 1,000 newborns do not survive the first month P(Neonatal Death) = 0.020

Probability: The fraction of times something happens out of the total. If 55 of 100 facilities are short-staffed, the probability of picking a short-staffed facility at random is 55/100 = 0.55.

Two ground rules that always hold:

  • Every probability is between 0 (never happens) and 1 (always happens)
  • The probabilities of all possible states add up to 1. If P(Low) = 0.55, then P(Adequate) = 1 - 0.55 = 0.45

Where Do These Numbers Come From?

From data:

Tanzania’s DHIS2 system (used at most facilities) and periodic facility surveys give us real counts – how many facilities have enough staff, how many have essential medicines, how many reported neonatal deaths.

When data exists, use it.

From expert judgment:

Sometimes the data is incomplete or missing. In those cases, experienced health workers, district officers, or program managers provide their best estimates. “I would say about 3 in 10 facilities in this region have functioning CPAP.”

When data is sparse, informed judgment fills the gap.

In practice, we use both. The numbers in this chapter are illustrative – clearly marked as such – but they are grounded in publicly available data on Tanzania’s health system (WHO, DHS, Lancet).

Conditional Probability

Given what we already know, what changes?

The Key Question

Plain probability asks: “What fraction of all facilities have high neonatal mortality?”

Conditional probability asks a sharper question:

“Given that a facility has low staffing, what fraction have high neonatal mortality?”

That word given changes everything. We are no longer looking at all 100 facilities. We are zooming in on just the 55 that are short-staffed and asking: among those, how many have high mortality?

A 2x2 Table of 100 Facilities

Imagine we survey 100 facilities in rural Tanzania and count how many fall into each combination of staffing and neonatal mortality:

NMR = High NMR = Low Row Total
Staffing = Low 33 22 55
Staffing = Adequate 9 36 45
Column Total 42 58 100

These are illustrative counts designed to reflect publicly available estimates of Tanzania’s ~55% workforce shortage and ~20/1,000 neonatal mortality rate.

Reading the Table

Now we can answer both the plain and conditional questions:

Plain probability:

P(NMR = High) = 42 / 100 = 0.42

Overall, 42 out of 100 facilities have high neonatal mortality.

Conditional probability:

P(NMR = High | Staffing = Low) = 33 / 55 = 0.60

Among the 55 short-staffed facilities, 33 have high mortality. That is 60%.

Compare: P(NMR = High | Staffing = Adequate) = 9 / 45 = 0.20

Among adequately staffed facilities, only 20% have high mortality. The gap between 60% and 20% is enormous – 40 percentage points. Staffing matters.

Conditional Probability: The Idea

Conditional Probability answers: “Among the cases where B is true, what fraction also have A?”

P(A | B) = (number with both A and B) / (number with B)

Crucial warning: P(NMR=High | Staffing=Low) and P(Staffing=Low | NMR=High) are not the same thing.

  • P(NMR=High | Staffing=Low) = 33/55 = 0.60 – “Of the short-staffed, 60% have high mortality”
  • P(Staffing=Low | NMR=High) = 33/42 = 0.79 – “Of the high-mortality facilities, 79% are short-staffed”

Mixing these up is one of the most common mistakes in health data analysis. Bayes’ rule (coming soon) is the tool that connects them correctly.

Lookup Tables (CPTs)

Your cheat sheet for how parents shape a child node

What Is a Lookup Table?

In Chapter 2, we drew arrows like Staffing –> Quality of Care. That arrow says staffing affects quality. But how much? A lookup table – formally called a Conditional Probability Table, or CPT – gives us the answer.

Lookup Table (CPT): A table that tells you the probability of each state of a child node, for every combination of its parent nodes. Think of it as: “If I know the parents, this table tells me what to expect from the child.”

This table is your cheat sheet. You look up the row that matches what you know about the parent variables, and the table tells you the probability of each outcome for the child variable. Every row adds up to 1.

CPT for Quality of Care

Suppose Quality of Care depends on two parent variables: Staffing and Essential Medicines. Here is the lookup table:

Staffing Essential Medicines P(Quality = Good) P(Quality = Poor)
Adequate Available 0.85 0.15
Adequate Unavailable 0.50 0.50
Low Available 0.45 0.55
Low Unavailable 0.15 0.85

How to read it: Find the row that matches the facility’s situation. If a facility has adequate staffing but essential medicines are unavailable, go to row 2: there is a 50/50 chance of good vs. poor quality care. If both staffing and medicines are lacking (row 4), there is only a 15% chance of good quality.

These probabilities are illustrative but grounded in published literature on care quality in low-resource settings. Tanzania reports low availability of essential medicines in many facilities (WHO Service Availability and Readiness Assessment).

CPT for Neonatal Mortality

Now the second link in the chain. Given quality of care, what is the probability of high vs. low neonatal mortality?

Quality of Care P(NMR = Low) P(NMR = High)
Good 0.82 0.18
Poor 0.35 0.65

Good quality care: 82% chance of low NMR. Quality care makes a huge difference.

Poor quality care: Only a 35% chance of low NMR. Nearly two in three facilities with poor care have high neonatal mortality.

Notice the structure. NMR depends only on Quality of Care in this table – not directly on Staffing or Medicines. Those upstream variables affect NMR, but only through Quality. The lookup table respects the arrows in our DAG.

Root Nodes Get Simple Tables

Nodes with no parents – root nodes – just need a single probability (no conditioning):

Variable P(Adequate / Available) P(Low / Unavailable)
Staffing 0.45 0.55
Essential Medicines 0.40 0.60

These reflect Tanzania’s reality: about 55% of facilities face staffing shortages, and essential medicine availability is low in many rural facilities.

A lookup table for every node = a complete quantitative model. Root nodes get a simple one-row table. Every other node gets a table conditioned on its parents. Put them all together, and the model can compute any probability you ask it.

Bayes’ Rule – Thinking Backwards

We see an outcome. What probably caused it?

The Backwards Question

So far we have been thinking forwards: given the causes, what outcome do we expect?

But in real life, managers often face the backwards question:

A district in Tanzania has high neonatal mortality. Before checking, you thought there was a 55% chance that any given facility is short-staffed. Now that you know mortality is high – what is the updated chance that staffing is the problem?

This is the kind of question Bayes’ rule answers. Let’s walk through it with natural frequencies – no formulas first, just counting.

Step 1: Start with 100 Facilities

Imagine 100 facilities. We know that about 55 are short-staffed and 45 have adequate staffing. That is our starting belief (before seeing any mortality data).

100
Facilities
–>
55
Low Staffing
45
Adequate Staffing

Step 2: How Many Have High NMR?

From our 2x2 table earlier, we know the mortality rates for each group:

  • Of the 55 short-staffed facilities: 60% have high NMR = 33 facilities
  • Of the 45 adequately staffed facilities: 20% have high NMR = 9 facilities
55 Low Staffing
33 High NMR
22 Low NMR
45 Adequate
9 High NMR
36 Low NMR

Total with high NMR: 33 + 9 = 42 facilities

Step 3: Among High-NMR Facilities, How Many Are Short-Staffed?

Now comes the key move. We have 42 facilities with high NMR. We zoom in on just those 42 and ask: how many are short-staffed?

Answer: 33 out of 42 = 0.79 (79%)

Before seeing the mortality data:

P(Low Staffing) = 55/100 = 0.55

We started with a 55% belief that a facility is short-staffed.

After learning NMR is high:

P(Low Staffing | NMR = High) = 33/42 = 0.79

The evidence pushed our belief up to 79%.

That is Bayes’ rule in action. Seeing high mortality is strong evidence of a staffing problem. Our belief jumped from 55% to 79% – a 24 percentage-point shift. No formulas needed, just careful counting.

The Tree Diagram

Here is the same logic drawn as a tree – a picture that makes the counting visible:

                        100 Facilities
                       /              \
              55 Low Staffing    45 Adequate Staffing
              /          \          /          \
        33 High NMR  22 Low NMR  9 High NMR  36 Low NMR

  Total High NMR = 33 + 9 = 42

  P(Low Staffing | High NMR) = 33 / 42 = 0.79

The tree diagram approach: Start at the top with your total. Branch by the cause you are interested in. Then branch again by the evidence you observed. Count the relevant leaves. Divide.

This is the same thing as Bayes’ formula, but you never have to memorize a formula. You just draw the tree and count.

Why Does This Matter?

Policy Implication

A district health officer in one of Tanzania’s 26 regions sees that a cluster of facilities has high neonatal mortality. The natural question is: why?

Before any investigation, the officer knows that staffing shortages affect about 55% of facilities nationally. But after seeing the mortality data, Bayes’ rule tells them: there is now a 79% chance the problem is staffing.

That updated belief can guide where to send the audit team first – and that matters when audit resources are scarce.

This is the logic behind mortality audits. Deaths are diagnostic signals. Bayes’ rule tells you how to update your beliefs about upstream causes when you observe a downstream outcome. It turns outcome data into actionable intelligence about what went wrong.

Bayes’ Rule: The General Pattern

For those who want to see the formula, here it is. But notice – it is just a compact way of writing the tree:

Bayes’ Rule:

P(Cause | Evidence) = P(Evidence | Cause) x P(Cause) / P(Evidence)

In our example:

  • P(Cause) = P(Low Staffing) = 0.55 – our starting belief
  • P(Evidence | Cause) = P(High NMR | Low Staffing) = 0.60 – how likely is the evidence if the cause is present
  • P(Evidence) = P(High NMR) = 0.42 – the total chance of seeing this evidence
  • P(Cause | Evidence) = (0.60 x 0.55) / 0.42 = 0.33 / 0.42 = 0.79 – our updated belief

You do not need to memorize this formula. If you can draw the tree and count, you get the same answer. The formula is just the shortcut.

Smart Diagrams – Bayesian Networks

A DAG that does math for you

What Is a Bayesian Network?

Bayesian Network: A DAG (the arrows from Chapters 2-3) plus a lookup table (CPT) for every node. Together, they form a model that can answer probability questions automatically.

DAG
(arrows)
+
Lookup Tables
(CPTs)
=
Bayesian
Network

Think of it this way: the DAG is the skeleton of the model – it shows the shape of the causal relationships. The lookup tables are the muscle – they give the model the numbers it needs to compute things. Put them together and you have a smart diagram that can answer “what if” questions.

What Can a Bayesian Network Do?

Once you have a Bayesian network, you can ask it questions like:

  • Forward: “If we improve staffing to adequate levels across the district, what happens to expected neonatal mortality?”
  • Backward: “We observe high mortality. What is the most likely cause – staffing, medicines, or both?”
  • What-if: “If essential medicines suddenly become available (but staffing stays low), how much does mortality improve?”

The network computes the answers using the lookup tables and the arrows. You do not have to do the math by hand – software (like R’s bnlearn package) handles it. But understanding the logic helps you trust the answers and catch mistakes.

The Key Rule

Each node only depends on its direct parents

The Rule That Simplifies Everything

Here is the single most important idea that makes Bayesian networks practical:

Each node only depends on its direct parents.

Once you know the parents of a node, nothing else in the network gives you additional information about that node.

Think of It This Way

Consider the chain: Staffing –> Quality of Care –> NMR

If you already know that Quality of Care is Poor, does it matter why it is poor? Whether it was caused by low staffing, missing medicines, or both – the probability of high NMR is the same. Quality of Care “screens off” everything upstream from NMR.

That is why the NMR lookup table only has a Quality column – not a Staffing column.

Why This Rule Matters: Fewer Numbers to Specify

Without this rule, we would need a huge table listing every possible combination of every variable:

Without the rule (brute force):

4 variables, each with 2 states = 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16 rows in a giant table.

10 variables? 1,024 rows.

20 variables? Over 1 million rows.

With the rule (Bayesian network):

Each node only needs parents in its table. Typical nodes have 1-3 parents, so each table has 2-8 rows.

20 variables with up to 3 parents each? About 160 rows total.

The DAG structure tells us which probabilities we can skip. Most variables are not directly connected, so we do not need to specify every possible combination. The causal structure does the work of simplifying the numbers.

The Rule in Our Tanzania Model

Let’s see this in our MNH example:

Staffing
P(Adequate)=0.45
Essential
Medicines
P(Available)=0.40
| |
Quality of Care
CPT: 4 rows
|
NMR
CPT: 2 rows

Quality of Care depends on Staffing and Medicines (its parents) – so its lookup table has 4 rows (2 x 2 combinations). NMR depends only on Quality (its sole parent) – so its table has just 2 rows. NMR does not need to know about Staffing or Medicines directly. The rule keeps things manageable.

MNH Application: Tanzania’s Health System

Building a Bayesian network with real-world structure

Tanzania at a Glance

Indicator Value Source
Maternal Mortality Ratio ~238 per 100,000 live births WHO
Neonatal Mortality Rate ~20 per 1,000 live births WHO
Regions 26 Government of Tanzania
Health workforce gap ~55% shortage WHO / Lancet
Health information system DHIS2 / GOTHOMIS at most facilities MoH Tanzania
Essential medicine availability Low in many rural facilities WHO SARA

Tanzania has made real progress – but significant gaps remain, especially in rural areas. The numbers below are illustrative, grounded in these publicly available estimates.

The Tanzania MNH Bayesian Network

We build a 4-node network with lookup tables for each node:

Nodes:

  • Staffing {Adequate, Low} – root node
  • Essential Medicines {Available, Unavailable} – root node
  • Quality of Care {Good, Poor} – depends on Staffing and Medicines
  • Neonatal Mortality {Low, High} – depends on Quality

Full Lookup Tables

Root nodes (starting probabilities):

Variable P(Adequate / Available) P(Low / Unavailable)
Staffing 0.45 0.55
Essential Medicines 0.40 0.60

Quality of Care | Staffing, Essential Medicines:

Staffing Medicines P(Quality = Good) P(Quality = Poor)
Adequate Available 0.85 0.15
Adequate Unavailable 0.50 0.50
Low Available 0.45 0.55
Low Unavailable 0.15 0.85

NMR | Quality of Care:

Quality P(NMR = Low) P(NMR = High)
Good 0.82 0.18
Poor 0.35 0.65

Querying the Model: Best vs. Worst Case

What can this network tell us? Let’s compare the best and worst scenarios:

Best case: Staffing = Adequate, Medicines = Available

P(Quality = Good) = 0.85

P(NMR = High) = 0.18 x 0.85 + 0.65 x 0.15

= 0.153 + 0.098 = 0.25

About 1 in 4 facilities still has high NMR – care is complex even in the best conditions.

Worst case: Staffing = Low, Medicines = Unavailable

P(Quality = Good) = 0.15

P(NMR = High) = 0.18 x 0.15 + 0.65 x 0.85

= 0.027 + 0.553 = 0.58

Nearly 3 in 5 facilities have high NMR when both inputs are missing.

The gap is 33 percentage points. Moving from worst case to best case cuts the probability of high NMR from 58% to 25%. That is the combined payoff of adequate staffing and available medicines.

Which Parent Matters More?

We can isolate each parent’s effect by fixing one and changing the other:

Scenario P(NMR = High) Change vs. Worst
Worst: Low Staff, No Medicines 0.58 –
Fix Staffing only: Adequate Staff, No Medicines 0.37 -0.21
Fix Medicines only: Low Staff, Has Medicines 0.44 -0.14
Best: Adequate Staff, Has Medicines 0.25 -0.33

Staffing has the larger individual effect – a 21 percentage-point reduction compared to 14 for medicines. In resource-constrained settings, workforce investment may yield greater returns.

But fixing both is better than the sum of fixing each alone. The combined improvement (33 pp) shows that staffing and medicines reinforce each other. A trained midwife with the right medicines can do far more than either resource alone.

  3. Using Bayes’ rule (or the tree approach): if a facility has high NMR, what is the probability it has low staffing?

R Workshop: Building a Bayesian Network

Using bnlearn to build, fill, and query the Tanzania model

R Block 1: Define the Network Structure

We start by telling R which nodes exist and which arrows connect them – the DAG skeleton.

# Load the bnlearn package (install it first if needed:
# install.packages("bnlearn"))
library(bnlearn)

# Define the DAG using a model string.
# Square brackets hold node names.
# A vertical bar "|" means "depends on."
# A colon ":" separates multiple parents.
#
# [Staffing]              = root node, no parents
# [Medicines]             = root node, no parents
# [Quality|Staffing:Medicines] = Quality depends on Staffing AND Medicines
# [NMR|Quality]           = NMR depends on Quality only

dag <- model2network(
  "[Staffing][Medicines][Quality|Staffing:Medicines][NMR|Quality]"
)

# Check what we built
dag                # prints the structure
nodes(dag)         # "Staffing" "Medicines" "Quality" "NMR"
arcs(dag)          # shows the 3 directed edges

Reading the model string: Each [...] block defines one node. If a node has parents, they appear after |. This is how bnlearn knows the shape of the DAG.

R Block 2: Fill In the Lookup Tables

Now we attach the CPTs we built on the earlier slides. Each lookup table is an R array.

# --- Root nodes: just a simple probability for each state ---

cpt_staffing <- array(
  c(0.45, 0.55),                    # P(Adequate), P(Low)
  dim = 2,
  dimnames = list(Staffing = c("Adequate", "Low"))
)

cpt_medicines <- array(
  c(0.40, 0.60),                    # P(Available), P(Unavailable)
  dim = 2,
  dimnames = list(Medicines = c("Available", "Unavailable"))
)

# --- Quality of Care: depends on Staffing and Medicines ---
# Each pair of numbers = P(Good), P(Poor) for one parent combo
# The order follows R's array filling: Staffing changes fastest

cpt_quality <- array(
  c(0.85, 0.15,    # Adequate staffing + Available medicines
    0.45, 0.55,    # Low staffing      + Available medicines
    0.50, 0.50,    # Adequate staffing + Unavailable medicines
    0.15, 0.85),   # Low staffing      + Unavailable medicines
  dim = c(2, 2, 2),
  dimnames = list(
    Quality   = c("Good", "Poor"),
    Staffing  = c("Adequate", "Low"),
    Medicines = c("Available", "Unavailable")
  )
)

# --- NMR: depends on Quality only ---

cpt_nmr <- array(
  c(0.82, 0.18,    # Good quality -> P(Low NMR), P(High NMR)
    0.35, 0.65),   # Poor quality -> P(Low NMR), P(High NMR)
  dim = c(2, 2),
  dimnames = list(
    NMR     = c("Low", "High"),
    Quality = c("Good", "Poor")
  )
)

# --- Combine everything into a fitted Bayesian network ---

bn_tz <- custom.fit(dag, list(
  Staffing  = cpt_staffing,
  Medicines = cpt_medicines,
  Quality   = cpt_quality,
  NMR       = cpt_nmr
))

# Check one of the tables
bn_tz$Quality    # prints the Quality lookup table

R Block 3: Query the Network

Now comes the payoff. We ask the network questions and it computes the answers.

# ----- Question 1: Overall probability of high NMR -----
# cpquery() uses simulation (sampling) to estimate probabilities.
# We set n = 1,000,000 samples for a stable answer.

cpquery(bn_tz,
  event    = (NMR == "High"),       # What we want to know
  evidence = TRUE,                  # No conditions -- overall
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: around 0.44 (44% of facilities have high NMR)

# ----- Question 2: P(NMR = High | Staffing = Low) -----
cpquery(bn_tz,
  event    = (NMR == "High"),
  evidence = (Staffing == "Low"),
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: around 0.52

# ----- Question 3: P(NMR = High | Adequate staff + Available meds) -----
cpquery(bn_tz,
  event    = (NMR == "High"),
  evidence = (Staffing == "Adequate" & Medicines == "Available"),
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: around 0.25

Exercise answers: Question 2 from the exercise = the first query above. The overall P(NMR = High) is about 0.44 – nearly half of facilities. The Bayesian network computed that by combining all four lookup tables automatically.

R Block 4: Bayes’ Rule in Action

Let’s use the network to answer our backwards question: given high NMR, what is the chance of low staffing?

# ----- Bayes' rule query -----
# "Given that we observe high NMR, what is the probability
#  that staffing is low?"

cpquery(bn_tz,
  event    = (Staffing == "Low"),    # Cause we are asking about
  evidence = (NMR == "High"),        # Evidence we observed
  n = 1e6
)
# Expected: around 0.68-0.70

# Compare to the prior (before seeing any evidence):
# P(Staffing = Low) = 0.55

# The evidence (high NMR) shifted our belief upward --
# from 55% to about 69%. High mortality is a signal
# that staffing is likely the problem.

Note: cpquery() uses random sampling, so answers vary slightly each run. For exact answers, you can use the gRain package (shown in the next block). Both give the same result – cpquery() is simpler, gRain is exact.

R Block 5: Exact Inference and Scenario Comparison

For precise answers (no randomness), we convert to the gRain package and compare intervention scenarios.

# Load gRain for exact probability calculations
library(gRain)

# Convert our bnlearn network to a gRain object
bn_grain <- as.grain(bn_tz)

# ----- Overall marginal probabilities -----
querygrain(bn_grain, nodes = "NMR")
querygrain(bn_grain, nodes = "Quality")

# ----- Scenario comparison: what if we intervene? -----
# "What if we ensure adequate staffing everywhere?"
# mutilated() sets a variable to a fixed value (the do-operator)

bn_do_staff <- mutilated(bn_tz,
  evidence = list(Staffing = "Adequate"))
querygrain(as.grain(bn_do_staff), nodes = "NMR")

# "What if we ensure medicines are available everywhere?"
bn_do_meds <- mutilated(bn_tz,
  evidence = list(Medicines = "Available"))
querygrain(as.grain(bn_do_meds), nodes = "NMR")

# "What if we fix both?"
bn_do_both <- mutilated(bn_tz,
  evidence = list(Staffing = "Adequate",
                  Medicines = "Available"))
querygrain(as.grain(bn_do_both), nodes = "NMR")

This is the payoff of the whole chapter. The mutilated() function implements the do-operator – it simulates an intervention by forcing a variable to a specific value. We can now compare “do nothing” vs. “fix staffing” vs. “fix medicines” vs. “fix both” and see exactly how much each intervention reduces the probability of high NMR.

R Block 6: Visualize the Network

# Option 1: bnlearn's built-in plot
graphviz.plot(bn_tz,
  main = "Tanzania MNH Bayesian Network",
  shape = "rectangle",
  highlight = list(
    nodes = "NMR",
    col = "#E24A3F",
    fill = "#E24A3F"
  )
)

# Option 2: dagitty + ggdag for publication-quality figures
library(dagitty)
library(ggdag)

tz_dag <- dagitty('dag {
  Staffing  [pos="0,0"]
  Medicines [pos="2,0"]
  Quality   [pos="1,1"]
  NMR       [pos="1,2"]
  Staffing  -> Quality
  Medicines -> Quality
  Quality   -> NMR
}')

ggdag(tz_dag) +
  theme_dag() +
  labs(title = "Tanzania MNH Causal Model (4 Nodes)")

Key Takeaways

Bayesian network = DAG + lookup tables. The DAG gives you the shape. The lookup tables give you the numbers. Together, they answer probability questions automatically.

  • Natural frequencies make probability intuitive: “55 out of 100 facilities are short-staffed”
  • Conditional probability sharpens our questions: “among short-staffed facilities, what fraction have high mortality?”
  • Lookup tables (CPTs) are your cheat sheets: find the row, read the probability
  • Bayes’ rule lets you think backwards: “we see a bad outcome; what probably caused it?” – use the tree diagram
  • The key rule – each node depends only on its direct parents – keeps the model manageable even as it grows
  • R + bnlearn lets you build, query, and compare intervention scenarios in a few lines of code
